subject: Specifying a Bias Field in INLA

messages.author: e14f84e392938414
messages.subject: Specifying a Bias Field in INLA
parts:
INLA Gurus,
Hello my name is Martin Arostegui. I am a postdoctoral scholar at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in the USA. I am very recently diving into the world of INLA, integrated species distribution models and so on. I came across this great 2020 paper in Ecography about different ways of accounting for bias in data collection. The two alternatives it discusses are 1) supplying a bias covariate or 2) including a second spatial field, which appear to be most appropriate when you have some but limited information on bias (but can supply at least one covariate) or effectively no information on bias whatsoever (and then use the second spatial field).

My question is, how might one in R-INLA best go about accounting for bias when you have really good knowledge of the bias distribution and can a priori map it spatially on the same grid as your occurrence data? In my case, I am hoping to use fishery-dependent data that provide a very accurate record of the uneven spatial effort distribution of the fishing fleet for over 20 yrs. I have been searching the relevant literature and the paper above comes closest to what I am aiming to do but I am hoping to more explicitly include a mapped bias field to better inform my integrated species distribution model and decrease its sensitivity to biases of the individual underlying datasets (particularly uneven spatial effort). Any insight you would be willing to share on how this is coded in R-INLA would be greatly appreciated and of enormous help!

Many Thanks,
Martin

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying a Bias Field in INLA
parts:
Hi Martin,

I think you mostly already answered your own question (apart from the
coding details). If you have a spatial field estimate (with spatially
varying mean and variance, and assuming some simple correlation
structure),
of the predictor bias, you can include the mean as a fixed offset in
the predictor, and add a random field component with the given
correlation (spde=inla.spde2.pcmatern() with prior.sigma=c(1,NA)) and
scaling weights given by the estimated bias standard deviation
(assuming bias_sigma and bias_mean have been evaluated at the
observation locations):
~ ... + f(bias_field, bias_sigma, model=spde) + offset(bias_mean)

In inlabru it would be similar (with all the make.A and inla.stack
code done internally):
~ ... + bias_field(coordinates, bias_sigma, model=spde) +
bias_mean(bias_mean, model="offset")

If the bias estimate is on the observation scale you'd need to work
out what that implies for the predictor and modified observation
model.
There are too many possibilities to say how to do that.

However, note that the likely effect of the above approach is
increased and complicated uncertainty, since the bias field and field
of interest can't be mutually identified; only their sum.
That may be what you need, but it also might not be...

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying a Bias Field in INLA
parts:
Finn,
Thanks for your quick and thorough reply. What I have, for example, is a presence-only dataset of where a given fish species was either marked or recaptured by the fishery. This is of course extremely biased in space by where fishers distributed their fishing effort. Given that it is presence-only I don't have a perfect effort estimation but I get a very good sense of the underlying effort bias from where all fish species in the database were either marked or recaptured. The number of these presence detections (across all species) are mapped out below and clearly biased to the NW Atlantic near the coast of New England:



How would you recommend going from a map like this to the bias correction in R-INLA code? Apologies for my lack of familiarity - this use case where I have excellent bias knowledge and want to specify it explicitly just seems very different than others where, for example, a single covariate is used to estimate only somewhat understood bias. Again, any and all help is immensely appreciated!

Many Thanks,
Martin
